question: A finance forum shared this: ten years of US unemployment, 2010 to 2019. The line climbs all decade. Where's the trick?
answer: In the axis, which runs upside down, with 10% at the bottom. Market analysts flip unemployment on purpose, so it rises with share prices on one chart, and mark it 'inverted' in small print. A screenshot loses the note. Right way up, unemployment fell every single year, from 9.6% to 3.7%.
move: Before reading a rise, check which end of the axis holds the big numbers.
ask: When a chart is shared without its notes, do I check which way each axis runs?

scene.headline: US unemployment, 2010 to 2019
scene.label: US unemployment rate, yearly
scene.found: Yes: the axis is upside down, with 10% at the bottom.
scene.miss: That part is fair. Read the numbers up the axis.

misses.marks: The line is true to its axis. Which way does the axis run?
misses.headline: A neutral title. The line is what says 'climbing'.

scene.name: The inverted axis
scene.lesson: Finance charts often flip one axis to make two lines match. Check its direction first.

source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPS
